title: Why Outside Money Loves a Primary
hook: A dollar spent in a low-turnout primary buys far more influence than the same dollar in a general election — which is where super PACs increasingly aim it.
key_points: Super PACs may raise and spend unlimited sums independently, but may not coordinate with a candidate's campaign.
Primaries are cheap targets: small electorates, weak party cues, and many voters meeting the names for the first time.
In safe seats the primary is effectively the election, so outside spending there decides who ultimately serves.
NPR reports super PACs spending more than $2 million in Alaska alone, aiming to work the state's unusual system to their candidate's benefit.
Alaska runs a top-four open primary feeding a ranked-choice general — a design that rewards strategy about who advances, not just who wins.
content_html: Campaign-finance debates usually picture a general election: two nominees, a national audience, expensive television. But the money that changes the most outcomes often lands earlier, in a party primary that most voters skip.
extra_html: Super PACs — committees that can raise and spend without limits so long as they do not coordinate with a candidate's own campaign — have leaned into that math. A primary electorate is small, the party label offers no way to tell the contenders apart, and many voters are encountering the names for the first time, so advertising does unusually heavy lifting. In a district safe for one party, the primary is not a preliminary round at all; it is the election. NPR's Liz Ruskin reports the pattern running through the 2026 midterm primaries, including Alaska, where super PACs have spent more than $2 million and, in NPR's telling, are trying to work the state's distinctive voting rules to their preferred candidate's advantage. Alaska sends the top four finishers from a single open primary to a ranked-choice general election, which shifts the strategic question from "who wins today" to "who else makes the final ballot" — a reminder that money follows the incentives a voting system creates.

related.title: The Distinction That Could Reshape Super PACs
related.hook: Citizens United protects unlimited independent spending. Maine's law doesn't touch spending — it caps what one donor may give the committee doing the spending. That gap is now in court.

related.title: How Votes Become Seats
related.hook: The same ballots can produce very different results depending on the electoral system used to count them.

related.title: Why Some Primaries Need a Second Round
related.hook: Win 34 percent of a crowded primary and in some states you're the nominee. In others, you go to a runoff — a rule that quietly reshapes which candidates survive.

related.title: Who Decides Which State Votes First?
related.hook: The order states vote in a presidential nominating contest isn't set by any constitution — it's a party rule, and parties rewrite it to change whose voters get courted first.

flashcards.prompt: What makes a primary an unusually efficient target for outside spending?
flashcards.back_html: Turnout is low and party labels give voters no guidance between same-party rivals — so a small amount of advertising moves a large share of the decisive electorate.

flashcards.prompt: What defines a super PAC's legal position?

choices.text: Unlimited independent spending, but no coordination with the candidate's campaign
Unlimited spending that must be coordinated with the campaign

flashcards.explanation_html: Independence from the campaign is the condition attached to the unlimited spending — the line the rules turn on.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a top-four primary feeding a ranked-choice general change spending strategy?

choices.text: Money can be aimed at who advances out of the primary, not only at winning it outright
It bans all outside spending in the primary round
It makes the general election result automatic

flashcards.explanation_html: When four candidates advance and voters then rank them, the useful question becomes which opponents make the final ballot.
